opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most interesting questions right now. Math is a really nice training ground because it's verifiable. You know when you got the right answer, so you can give the model a clean signal. But what you're actually teaching isn't really "math" in the narrow sense. It's things like breaking a hard problem into smaller pieces, trying an approach, noticing when it isn't working, backtracking, and checking your own work before you commit to an answer.

Those habits turn out to be pretty general. When we look at how models handle things like coding, scientific reasoning, or even messier tasks like analyzing a legal document or planning a multi-step project, a lot of the same moves show up. The model pauses, considers alternatives, and catches its own mistakes. I don't think it's that the model learned calculus and now applies calculus to law. It's more that it learned *how to think carefully* when the answer isn't obvious.

That said, transfer isn't automatic or complete. Real-world domains have ambiguity that math doesn't. There's often no single right answer, you need domain knowledge, and you have to make judgment calls about what matters to the person you're helping. So a big part of my work is building evaluations that test whether these reasoning gains actually show up on economically meaningful, realistic tasks, the kind of work professionals really do, rather than just on benchmarks that look like math competitions. Sometimes the transfer is surprisingly strong, and sometimes it shows us exactly where we still need better data or training signals.

So my short answer is that math teaches the discipline of reasoning, and that discipline transfers a lot. But to be truly useful in other domains, you still need grounding in how those domains actually work.

r001.rationale: The response says that useful transfer to other domains still requires grounding in how those domains work, alongside domain knowledge and judgment. This communicates the need for domain-specific support to realize the benefits.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's actually one of the main reasons we focus so much on math as a training and evaluation domain, even though most people are not going to ask a model to prove a theorem in their day-to-day life.

The thing about math is that it's one of the few domains where you have a really clean signal about whether reasoning was correct. In most areas, if someone gives you an argument, it's hard to tell whether it's right. In math, you can check. And so what you end up learning when you train on math isn't really "math facts," it's a set of habits. Things like: decompose the problem into pieces, keep track of what you've actually established versus what you're assuming, notice when a step doesn't follow, backtrack when you hit a contradiction, verify your answer at the end. Those are very general skills.

And we do see that transfer empirically. When we improved reasoning on math and competition-style problems, we saw gains on things that look nothing like math, like coding, like scientific question answering, even some of the softer evaluations where the model has to plan or follow a complicated set of instructions. The model gets better at being careful. It's less likely to just pattern-match to a plausible-sounding answer, and more likely to actually work through the problem.

That said, I'd be a little careful about overclaiming. Transfer isn't perfect. There are domains, like a lot of real-world professional tasks, where the hard part isn't the logical reasoning at all. It's ambiguity, it's knowing what the person actually wants, it's dealing with messy information where there isn't a single right answer. Math doesn't teach you much about that. So I think of math as building the "rigor" muscle, and then you need other kinds of data and other kinds of evaluation to build the "judgment" muscle. You really want both.

But if I had to pick one domain to get really good at as a foundation for everything else, I'd still pick math. It's the cleanest way we have to teach a system what it means to actually be right.

r001.rationale: The response says math does not teach ambiguity and that other kinds of data and evaluation are needed to build judgment. It does not clearly state that realizing the benefits may require scaffolding specific to the target domain.

astra-6.text:
I think math is a useful training ground for reasoning because it gives you problems where you can check whether you got the answer right. But getting there requires skills that are much more general: breaking a problem into smaller pieces, deciding which approach to try, keeping track of assumptions, and recognizing when you need to backtrack.

Those skills can be useful in coding, for example, where you have to work through dependencies and check whether your solution actually works. The interesting question is whether you’ve learned a particular mathematical technique or a more general way of approaching problems. Transfer isn’t automatic, but learning to reason through math can give you a foundation for tackling problems in other domains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think math is a useful training ground for reasoning because you get a clear signal about whether an approach worked. But the skills you develop along the way—breaking a problem into smaller pieces, keeping track of assumptions, checking your work, and trying a different approach when you get stuck—are useful well beyond math.

In coding, for example, you can break a task into steps, write a solution, and test it. In a more open-ended domain, you might need to weigh evidence or recognize that you don’t have enough information yet. The interesting question is whether you’ve learned a particular procedure or a more general ability to reason. Getting better at math alone doesn’t establish that transfer; you have to look at how you do on problems in those other domains.
